strengths: The paper addresses an important evaluation problem for brain-to-text decoding: repeated stimuli across participants and overlapping fMRI windows can produce overly optimistic estimates of generalization.

Separating subject overlap from stimulus overlap is useful. The intended evaluation on both unseen subjects and unseen stimuli is meaningful, and grouping fMRI data by story offers a sensible way to avoid overlapping text windows.

The experiments cover two modalities, two public datasets, and two established decoding systems. Comparing five existing splitting strategies and reporting overlap measurements across four seeds provides useful breadth.
weaknesses: The published algorithms do not enforce the central zero-leakage guarantee. Algorithm 1, line 15, checks subject membership but permits adding an edge to a held-out text; Algorithm 2, line 33, checks task membership but permits adding a held-out subject. The initialization also conflicts with the prose about which nodes receive an edge. These may be implementation-description errors, but corrected pseudocode and verified pairwise disjointness are essential.

The quantitative validation contains substantial inconsistencies. Equation 8 measures intersection of individual signals, whereas the stated concern is overlap of subject identities; its denominator is also zero for completely held-out subjects. Table 4 reports EEG2Text ROUGE-1 recall of 23.98, precision of 23.95, and F-score of 25.74, which is incompatible with standard, consistently aggregated F1. Similar discrepancies occur in Table 3. The metric definitions and reported results require an audit.

The experiments do not isolate the claimed damage from leakage. Improving evaluation scores or decreasing validation loss with longer training does not itself establish overfitting. Table 2 changes encoder initialization, learning rate, and training duration together, while different splits change subjects, stimuli, and potentially training-set size. Matched comparisons and decoder-only or shuffled-signal controls are needed to support the conclusions about memorization and the encoder's limited contribution.

The blanket characterization of alternative protocols as leakage is too broad. Evaluating unseen text for a previously observed subject is a legitimate task. Joint subject-and-stimulus holdout measures a different generalization target; failure to satisfy it does not automatically invalidate evaluations designed for other targets. The paper should distinguish actual sample contamination from subject overlap and qualify its claims about prior work.

The stated improvements in dataset utilization and generalization are not demonstrated. No retained-data fractions or comparisons with simple joint group holdouts are reported. Extending a graph after fixing assignments does not establish globally maximum data retention, and imposing a harder evaluation split does not itself improve model generalization.

Reproducibility remains insufficient for the proposed benchmark. Appendix A provides useful hyperparameters, but the manuscript supplies no release link or exact split manifests, post-filtering partition sizes, or clear inference protocol establishing whether reference prefixes are used. Four seeds cover overlap measurements, while decoding results lack uncertainty across training runs or held-out subject/story selections. Together with the algorithm and metric inconsistencies, these concerns require correction and re-evaluation before a sound Findings recommendation; resubmission next cycle is appropriate.
